issues.legal_issue: Forest officials’ permission to continue forest work did not transfer ownership of trees where no valid sale or authorized extension of the contracts was made.
material_facts: In one group, the forest contracts had expired before the officials allowed further work; the officials’ authority to execute contracts did not itself authorize them to sell State property, and no duly authorized sale or completed contract followed.

In the other groups, permission to cut trees had been granted only for a period ending before the petitioners’ later work, and no fresh permission or valid contract authorizing that work was established.
The petitioners relied on acts of forest officials, but the record did not establish that the State had ratified an unauthorized sale.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners acquired no legal ownership of the trees through the forest officials’ permissions or purported extensions.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer of State forest produce requires a sale or grant by an authority empowered to make it; authority merely to execute contracts on behalf of the State does not confer power to authorize the sale. The Court distinguished Chatturbhuj Vithaldas v. Moreshwar Parashram, 1954 SCR 817 : AIR 1954 SC 236, because no ratification was shown, and held that section 6 of the Abolition of Jagirs Act did not assist where the contracts had expired before the property was allegedly acquired.

predicates.forest_work_authorized_only_by_official_: The claimant continued or began forest work on the basis of permission or action by forest officials.
predicates.contract_period_expired: The relevant contract had expired before the claimant undertook the work from which ownership was claimed.
predicates.prior_permission_period_expired: The permission for cutting trees had ended before the claimant undertook the work from which ownership was claimed.
predicates.no_authorized_sale_or_extension: No sale, grant, or extension authorizing the transfer of the forest produce was made by an authority empowered to do so.

issues.definition: When forest work rests only on officials’ permission after the relevant contract or cutting permission has ended, and no empowered authority makes a sale or extension, the claimant obtains no legal title to the forest produce.

issues.legal_issue: A bare licence to work in a forest, or permission that merely avoids penalties under forest legislation, does not transfer ownership of trees or forest produce.
material_facts: The forest officials permitted the petitioners to enter and work in the forest, but lacked authority to grant the trees to them.

The petitioners relied on statutory provisions concerning permitted acts in reserved and protected forests, but the Court found no basis for concluding that the relevant forests had been declared under those provisions and held that the provisions did not deal with the sale of forest produce.
The permissions did not include a grant of the trees or other movable forest produce.
issues.conclusion: The licence and forest-law permissions did not pass ownership of the trees or products made from them to the petitioners.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Easements Act defines a licence as a right to do something on another’s immovable property without creating an interest in that property. A licence can transfer movable property only if it is coupled with a grant of that property; Ramakrishna v. Unni Check, I.L.R. 16 Mad. 280, involved such a grant in the terms of the licence. Sections 26(2)(a) and 34 of the Madhya Bharat Forest Act concern permission to do otherwise prohibited acts or relief from penalties; they do not transfer title to forest produce.

predicates.forest_work_licence_only: The claimant was given permission to enter or work in forest land without a grant of the produce.
predicates.no_grant_of_forest_produce: The permission did not include a grant transferring ownership of the trees or other forest produce.
predicates.no_authority_to_grant_forest_produce: The person granting permission lacked authority to transfer ownership of the forest produce.

issues.definition: A claimant given only permission to work in a forest, without a grant of the produce by someone authorized to make it, obtains no property title through that permission.

issues.legal_issue: A petition asserting a fundamental right to hold and dispose of property cannot be maintained when the petitioner has not acquired the property claimed.
material_facts: The petitioners sought relief under Article 32, claiming that the State was preventing them from holding and disposing of timber, charcoal, kattha, and other forest produce.
The Court concluded that no legal transfer of ownership of the trees or the resulting products to the petitioners had occurred.
The claimed fundamental right depended on the forest produce being the petitioners’ property.
issues.conclusion: The petitioners could not maintain the petitions on the asserted fundamental-rights ground, and the petitions were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A petition under Article 32 is not maintainable unless the petitioner establishes a fundamental right. The asserted right to hold and dispose of property could not support these petitions because ownership of the claimed forest produce had not passed to the petitioners.

predicates.article_32_fundamental_rights_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of a fundamental right.
predicates.property_right_claimed: The claimant asserted a fundamental right to hold and dispose of particular property.
predicates.no_legal_title_to_claimed_property: The claimant had not legally acquired ownership of the property on which the asserted right depended.

issues.definition: A constitutional petition asserting a fundamental right to property is not maintainable on that claim when the claimant has not legally acquired the property.
